messages.subject: JAGS samplers
messages.body_plain:
Posting this here in case it is useful to someone: I recently had a question about the samplers that JAGS uses to estimate blavaan models. For a given model, information about this can be found relatively easily (assuming that "fit" is your blavaan model):

## get the underlying runjags object:
jagsmodel <- blavInspect(fit, 'mcobj')

extract(jagsmodel, 'samplers')

You will typically see slice samplers and conjugate normal samplers.

Ed

messages.subject: gamma prior for precision under target="stan"
messages.subject_clean: gamma prior for precision under target="stan"
messages.body_plain:
I have noticed some unusual results when specifying a gamma
prior for a variance when target=“stan” as compared to target=“stanclassic”. I
have seen this in a few situations. An example is given below, in which the
analytical solution is known. Following on my previous thread about potential
differences between using target=“stan” as compared to target=“stanclassic”, I
am now using the development version of blavaan from github, as linked at the bottom
of https://github.com/ecmerkle/blavaan.

The example comes from Levy & Mislevy (2016, Bayesian Psychometric Modeling), section
4.26. The situation is a model for a single normally distributed variable with
known mean and unknown variance (or precision, or standard deviation). The
model specifies the known mean of 80. The prior for the unknown variance is
Inv-Gamma(5, 150); equivalently, the prior for the unknown precision is Gamm(5,
150). The dataset has 10 values: 91, 85, 72, 87, 71, 77, 88, 94, 84, 92. The
analytical posterior for the variance is an Inv-Gamma(10, 534.5), which has
posterior mean of 59.39 and posterior standard deviation of 21.00.

In specifying this model via blavaan, I wasn’t able to fix the
mean. To get around this, I specified a N(80, .001) prior (in the sd metric)
for the mean. And I attempted to specify a Gamma(5, 150) prior for the
precision

Code for the model is:

library(blavaan)

test.data <-
as.data.frame(c(91, 85, 72, 87, 71, 77, 88, 94, 84, 92))

colnames(test.data)
<- "x"

# Define the model
in lavaan expressions ------

blavaan.model.expressions.stan
<- '

  # "Equation" for the model

  # This specifies a mean (intercept) for the
variable

  x ~ prior("normal(80,.001)")*1

  # Variance for the  variable

  x ~~ prior("gamma(5,150)[prec]")*x

'

Fitting the model with target=“stanclassic” yields results
for the variance that are in line with the analytical solution. Code and
results follow.

fitted.model.stan.classic
<- blavaan(blavaan.model.expressions.stan, n.chains=1, sample=50000,
target="stanclassic",
test="none", data=test.data)

blavInspect(fitted.model.stan.classic,
'mcobj')

               mean se_mean    sd
2.5%    25%    50%
75%  97.5% n_eff Rhat

nu[1,1,1]     80.00
0.00  0.00  80.00
80.00  80.00  80.00
80.00 53383    1

theta[1,1,1]  59.52
0.21 21.04  31.37  44.82
55.29  69.53 111.39  9841
1

lp__         -22.92    0.01
0.99 -25.58 -23.32 -22.62 -22.21 -21.95 14025    1

Fitting the model with target=“stan” yields results for the variance
that are meaningfully different. It seems there are more extreme values, yielding
a larger mean, standard deviation, and higher percentiles. Code and
results follow.

fitted.model.stan
<- blavaan(blavaan.model.expressions.stan, n.chains=1, sample=50000,
test="none", data=test.data)

blavInspect(fitted.model.stan,
'mcobj')

               mean se_mean    sd
2.5%    25%    50%
75%  97.5% n_eff Rhat

Theta_var[1]  71.16
0.29 26.83  35.49  52.50
65.75  83.59 138.68  8773
1

Nu_free[1]    80.00
0.00  0.00  80.00
80.00  80.00  80.00
80.00 54522    1

lp__         -26.02    0.01
0.99 -28.68 -26.41 -25.72 -25.31 -25.05 12963    1

I am unsure as to why this difference occurs. Can
you advise?

Thanks,

Roy

messages.subject: Re: Calculated quantities without labels
messages.body_plain:
Robin,

I don't think it is possible to use ":=" without specifying labels. You could double-check that on the lavaan google group, because blavaan is using lavaan's syntax for the defined parameters.

But you could also calculate those things yourself, using the posterior samples. If your model is called "fit":

draws <- blavInspect(fit, "draws")
## convert from list to matrix
draws <- do.call("rbind", draws)

and now you just have to apply your operations to the columns of draws that you want. The draws column names use the parameter names from the Stan file; to figure out what corresponds to what, do this:

with(parTable(fit), cbind(lhs, op, rhs, pxnames))

And then you might have, for example

total <- draws[,'bet_sign[2]'] + draws[,'bet_sign[1]'] * draws[,'bet_sign[3]']
summary(total)

Ed

>

As Ed said, would be useful to see the model and call for blavaan.

A couple of thoughts, to get the CFI/TLI from the blavFitIndices you need to provide the estimated null/baseline model to the fnction, see the example in the ?blavFitIndices page

If this is the case, the adjustment based on the effective estimated parameters pD will lead to a negative df in the RMSEA formula which causes the NaNs.
